Network ACLs

The topic is now confirmed by the project owner, so the technical article is populated. The canonical ledger status is not promoted until the original published artifact is recovered.

Network ACLs add stateless allow/deny filtering at the subnet boundary, complementing rather than replacing stateful Security Groups.

Architecture / mental model

subnet boundary → numbered NACL rules (allow/deny, stateless) → network interface → Security Group → workload

How it works

A Network ACL is associated with one or more subnets and evaluates traffic crossing the subnet boundary. Rules are numbered and evaluated in order until a matching rule is found.

Unlike Security Groups, NACLs are stateless. Allowing an inbound request does not automatically allow the return traffic, so both directions and ephemeral return ports must be considered when designing restrictive rules.

NACLs can explicitly deny traffic, which makes them useful for coarse subnet-level controls or emergency blocking, while Security Groups remain the more common workload-level allow policy.

Hands-on reference

aws ec2 describe-network-acls
aws ec2 describe-subnets --query 'Subnets[].[SubnetId,VpcId,AvailabilityZone]' --output table

Verification

Map the workload subnet to its associated NACL, inspect inbound and outbound rule numbers, then test a known allowed flow and a deliberately blocked flow while accounting for return traffic.

Field note / gotcha

Because NACLs are stateless, opening only the destination service port in one direction can still break the connection when the response path/ephemeral ports are denied.

Security considerations

Use NACL denies carefully: a broad low-numbered rule can black-hole legitimate subnet traffic before later allow rules are ever evaluated.

What I learned

Security Groups and NACLs protect different boundaries. Understanding statefulness is the difference between deliberate policy and mysterious timeouts.
